utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I hope that you have before you a small disclosure note in relation to what occurred yesterday evening and this morning for Dr. Bosanac. My learned friends have got copies of the note, and perhaps the document speaks more eloquently than I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That being the case, we would seek to call Dr. Bosanac in relation to what I will call the blue file index and for her to give evidence in relation to this matter. It may well be -- can I just indicate what the professor apparently has said is that they have not looked at those documents for some considerable time. The fax paper tends to lose the printing ability or hold its message, and they were photocopies taken of that. So what has been done at the moment is checks are being made to see whether the documents are actually fully in existence, although it's believed that the vast majority are. Certainly as far as we are concerned, we would try and prioritise and ask for the individuals who are named on the Annex A of the indictment, for -- if there are any files in relation to those individuals, for that to be revealed. And if needs be, and with obviously the leave of the Court, perhaps to call the professor to give evidence on the methodology that was used, unless my friends are now satisfied. The problem that I see may well be one of translation, although I believe it's correct to say that it would have almost certainly gone off in B/C/S; and therefore, that should not create insurmountable problems. So the final submission that we would make is that we would seek to call Dr. Bosanac in relation to the blue file and the additional two documents that were revealed to the Defence as Christmas. There is another file that we are not going to rely on this -- at this juncture, but my learned friends are aware of its existence and have it served on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if required by the Defence, you propose to call a further witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we would -- if the Defence require it, we would, I would have thought, try and locate the person we believe is most suitable to deal with this area of the compilation of material and to call evidence in relation to that, if it's needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone. I have heard the explanation of my learned friend. It's just that I think that from this letter it follows clearly that the documentation exists, in part in photocopied fax messages and another part in stored electronic messages, so there is no problem. That is, indeed, why the Defence presented its request yesterday, to verify the documentation we have received based on the original documents, and we would appreciate it if our learned friends from the Prosecution could do that, namely, request the documentation from the Ministry of Health in the Republic of Croatia. We will examine the witness. Professor Ivica Kostovic I see is mentioned here who has processed this documentation. I suppose that is the person I have in mind. As for the witness, Mrs. Bosanac, the Defence has no objection to her being examined by the Prosecution to these circumstances. The only question in our mind is whether it would be possible to cross-examine her on the contents of the blue notebook, which seems to be the basis for the documentation we have asked to be requested. So we understand that she could be questioned about the technicalities, but we would also like to cross-examine her on the contents. And perhaps we should even examine Mr. Kostovic, Professor Ivica Kostovic, if the Prosecution has no objection to that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a very brief, specific suggestion. I fully accept the proposal of the Prosecution to hear Witness Bosanac now in chief, that we cross-examine her on these documents under Rule 68, and I completely agree that when we receive the documentation, either she or Professor Kostovic confirm that side of the facts with a proviso that if the Defence would reserve the right to question Mrs. Bosanac later after we receive the documents and see if there is anything relevant to her, as long as we have a relevant witness in these proceedings that could be examined on these documents. But without having seen them, we cannot give a decided answer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand from his clear signal that Mr. Borovic has nothing that he wishes to add to what has been said by Mr. Vasic and Mr. Lukic. Is there any difficulty you see from what has been said, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would have thought not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The position will be that the Chamber will hear Dr. Bosanac now and she will be cross-examined. If it then is considered by the Defence that there is need to cross-examine her further or to hear another witness, that can be specifically raised, and it will be ruled upon in light of the circumstances as they appear at the time. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I please call Dr. Bosanac, who I believe is in the waiting-room outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Bosanac, welcome back. May we ask you once again to take the affirmation that is on the card? It's been such a long time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, you may remember that you gave evidence in October - a long time ago - and that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a CD which had within it a number or a large number of details about individuals who had been to the hospital, and it dealt with their administrative -- their administration. Do you remember that? It recorded things like names, occupation, date of entry, and diagnosis. Now, do you remember providing OTP with that particular document, or with that compact disc?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your CD actually comes out like this when printed. You will be relieved to know I will not be asking you any details about that, but what I have had done, I have had compiled a list which is in a blue folder beside you on the left-hand side. Could you just reach for it, please? And would you be kind enough to open it? And I just want to deal with the actual, not the first page, but the actual second page. So not the coloured page, because that's an index. Yes. The next one. Now, you can see on the left-hand side a space where various names were originally included. Do you see that? Now, would you be kind enough, please, if you look at the bottom right-hand corner, you get the page numbers. So if you look to the bottom right-hand corner and go to page 3 and 4, I'd just like to direct your attention to one or two matters. Now, page 3 should have on it -- approximately one-third of the way down, there is a name in that column. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then if we turn over the page we can see that there are again names, one of them coloured. To assist you, I think it's right to say that when you gave this CD and details to the Office of the Prosecutor, it was on the basis that many of the people whose names were recorded here were still living and you felt bound by medical privilege that their details should not be released. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: However, the names that we find occasionally marked in these pages are individuals that the Prosecution say these people were buried at Ovcara, just to give the context for you. Now, can we deal, please, with the method of recording of individuals who came to the hospital throughout 1991? And clearly in 1991 there was a period of peace, and then matters got a little worse. And at the end, before the fall of Vukovar, it was extremely difficult. But could you please, in very general terms, explain to the Court how it was if a person came to the hospital they were recorded or their names were recorded and registered within the -- the documents of the hospital? Can you do that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody would come to the hospital - in those months of the year 1991, there were mostly wounded - they would first go through the emergency admission department, emergencies. If the person was able to speak, their personal details would be recorded, their full name, date of birth, a working diagnosis would be made, and the admitting doctor would decide whether the person would go immediately to X-rays, examination, surgery, or if there was a wound, it had to be dressed. And after that the patient would be either hospitalised or sent home or to one of the shelters in town. Every day, pursuant to the protocol prevailing in the infirmary, the protocol of surgeries and inpatients, we would type into the computer the name and surname of every patient, father's name, date of birth, place of injury, and diagnosis, and initially we would send it by e-mail to the information section of the Ministry of Health. When in the beginning of November that communication was broken, then we typed the lists on a typewriter and sent them by fax, again to the information section of the Ministry of Health headquarters. Every patient had his or her chart indicating existence of fever, procedures undertaken, surgeries, if any, and developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask you, please, to look at the top line of -- well, actually perhaps a better example is if we go to page 3, and we have got the name of Babic, Drazen. So bottom right-hand corner, page 3. Can we deal, please, with what the headings at the top of each column means? So obviously the first column relates to what, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first column is the title of that person, ZNG means Home Guard Corps. It was actually an organisation that later developed into the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have got on the third column, "Datum," and then another word, what does that prefer to, please? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Date of wounding or date of injury. The means the date when the injury or wound was sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move to column four, "Mjesto," and again that column.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Place of injury or wounding, the place where it was sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then clearly number five is diagnosis. Do you know, out of interest, exactly what this diagnosis refers to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means "vulnus explosivum genus sinistri." That means a blast wound to the left knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then we have an entry, which is "Datum Unosa." What does that refer to, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Date of entry, meaning entry of data into that database. That means this information was sent by us, and entered into this database of wounded persons on the 25th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then the final column, please, column 7, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seventh column relates to the area of origin of that person or perhaps organisation. In this case we have the place name Nasice, it's a small place between Vukovar and Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with one or two other matters, and I will remain on page 3, if I may. If we go to the top of page 3, we can see clearly that there is no name entered. We have got then the title, which is Civodr, then we have the date of wounding. Now, in this instance there is no date of wounding and there is no diagnosis, and that is not the only time that that occurs. Can we deal firstly with the absence of diagnosis on some of the entries that we see throughout this document? Why was it that diagnosis was not entered on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, could I ask you just to stop for a moment, please? We have a system in this Court where your words are then transposed into English and French, and unfortunately the machine isn't working, certainly my machine isn't working. And therefore, we have no record of what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I can her the interpreter now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it is now through. There was no interpretation for that last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall I ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can it be confirmed whether it has reached the transcript? No, it hasn't. It will need to be given again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask it word for word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, I'll ask the question again, if you wouldn't mind. Can I deal with one or two other matters, and I'll remain on page 3, if I may. If we go to the top of page 3, we can clearly see that there is no name entered. We have got then the title, which is Civodr, and then we have the date of wounding. Now, in this instance there is no date of wounding and there is no diagnosis, and that is not the only time that that occurs in this document. So can we deal firstly with the absence of diagnosis on some of the entries that we can see throughout the document itself? Why was it that the diagnosis was not entered on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was because of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Once again, we need to stop, we are not get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder whether we would hear the English interpreter's voice, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we can now. Thank you. I'm afraid we must try again, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll not read it; I will try and ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, on page 3 - we'll try one more time - and we take the top line, we can see that there is no name clearly there for obvious reasons, but there is no date of wounding and there is no diagnosis. When one looks through this document you find on several occasions, or many occasions, that there is no diagnosis recorded. Are you able to help us why it is that the diagnosis section is blank?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- or rather, I believe I can explain that there is no diagnosis because the lists of wounded persons were not always compiled by medical staff only. This was also done by police officers in their special section for wounded persons. It was a special section within the MUP police administration. What they needed was the person's first and last names as well as the place where the person was wounded; likewise, the Vukovar ICR, International Red Cross, also compiled lists with persons' first and last name as well as the place of wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with this document itself? My understanding - and please can you just clarify whether I'm right or wrong about this - that this document only relates to either people who are wounded or people who are ill. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when one has an absence of diagnosis, it doesn't mean that the person was not wounded or not ill. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about the completion of the document; you have told us that sometimes it would be the police, the Red Cross, and perhaps other persons. Why was it that individuals who were not medically trained were compiling this -- or compiling this material? Because clearly sometimes there is diagnosis and sometimes there isn't. Can you explain to us the circumstances that were existing at the hospital which caused the absence of diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke earlier on about the circumstances under which we had to perform our duties. There would sometimes be as many at 90 new wounded on a given day. All of the medical staff were busy seeing to it that these patients got proper medical attention. It wasn't always possible to enter into this database everything that was written down when patients were admitted, everything that was written down in their case histories, everything that the anaesthetics people wrote down. It wasn't that often that it was possible for some of the medical staff to use this database in order to include this new information. The top priority was to have all the information forwarded as quickly as possible to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That brings me on to my next question, which relates to the forwarding of the information to Zagreb. Why was the information forwarded to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because those were our instructions -- or rather, our agreement with the information office of Croatia's health ministry. They said that we should do our best to forward all information from the hospital as quickly as possible, pass it on to Zagreb so that their information would be as accurate as possible as to what exactly was going on, how many wounded were being admitted each day. And the police section that I spoke about had the same assignment, but all they sent was the first and last names, the place of wounding. They had special lists for those wounded and special lists for those killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the method of transmission? How did you send it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already pointed out, we had a computer which was set up in August for the hospital's use. We used e-mail to forward all sorts of information, not just this type of information, but also whatever our needs happened to be at the time in terms of medical equipment, in terms of medicine. However, in early November, sometime around the 6th of November, I believe, this line of communication was disrupted, making it impossible for us to forward information like this. So we just typewrote our reports and faxed them. There was a fax machine at the Vukovar defence headquarters; that was the only fax machine that was still operating in the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal then, please, with the original, what we now call hard copy, the original paper -- papers that were within the hospital that were records of patients. What happened to those records, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the records remained at the hospital when the troops arrived. In 1997 upon our return to Vukovar, we found none of those records. Some still exist, I mean some of the original records, but we only managed to obtain this at a later stage. These records are in relation to those wounded who had been taken to other hospitals in Croatia before the siege was complete as well as in relation to those wounded who left town on the 18th of October convoy organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres. There are a number of hospitals, such as one in Koprivnica, the one in Virovitica, or the Zagreb clinical centre who later sent us the medical records in relation to the wounded who left town on that convoy. However, concerning all of those who had not yet left town and who were still in the hospital on the 20th of November as well as those whose information had been recorded in the hospital records previously, including their case histories, protocol, and any painkillers that were administered, we found no records or documents about those patients. All of those records were taken to Belgrade after the fall of Vukovar along with the computer that was there. Later on I read something about this in an interview by [as interpreted] Dr. Stankovic; that was after the fall of Vukovar. He worked as a pathologist, and he identified some of the bodies in Vukovar. I personally spoke to him when we had the negotiations in Hungary in 1992, negotiations concerning the missing persons. They had all the records; they probably still have those, as we speak. Dr. Stankovic, I read, has recently become Defence minister in Serbia and Montenegro. If there is any further interest from the Court on this issue, I believe he will make himself available and perhaps testify to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I ask then please about the accuracy of the document that you received back from Zagreb. The first question is this: You obtained, I believe, a compact disc from Zagreb containing these records. When was that; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was back in 1997 on our return to Vukovar. We received a CD containing this information. I had requested our information office to make copies of those documents, thinking that we would be needing them. There are still quite many people requesting certificates about the original circumstances of their wounding, those people, all of those who were in Zagreb at the time, those who still live as refugees, all of those who had been wounded. For example, recently I received a request from a gentleman who was wounded and his left leg was blown off. He remained in Vukovar during the occupation; he's still there. He wanted to have a new certificate now. We tracked down his information in our database, and we were thus able to issue an accurate certificate on the original circumstances on his wounding so that he may now obtain some of his entitlements as a victim of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Clearly you did not know all the patients who were in your hospital at Vukovar in November of 1991, but have you had an opportunity to look at the collated material from Zagreb and try to ascertain whether it is accurate or not and corresponds with your memory?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether you believe that the collated material from Zagreb is accurate or not and why.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the material that I've gone through, not all of it though - simply because there is so much information in relation to that particular year, but I can talk about those patients who I know were there, those patients I know personally. In relation to those, I can say that this material is accurate. Information is not very detailed, though; there is only four types of information there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the individuals that you recognise, did -- and the injuries specified, did that correspond with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you were to estimate the number of people that you can remember, the injuries that they had, and the actual collated material, what sort of number would you be talking about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how many recorded wounded persons in those documents? Do you mean how many or what different types of information I was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'm really trying to ascertain if, for example, you were able to remember 20 or 30 people, and then you look at the collated material, whether that collated material corresponds with your memory, with your recollection. If you're not able to say, do say so.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very specific. I would need to give it some thought. I would need to go back to the original documents to check the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, I think it's right to say, and indeed the Court are aware, that yesterday, last evening, and I think also this morning, you contacted Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the purpose of that phone call was to ascertain what happened at Zagreb and whether the material that was sent electronically to Zagreb was still retained there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you spoke, I think, to Professor Kostovic. Would you be kind enough, please, to tell us who Professor Kostovic is.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Ivica Kostovic is director of the brain institute, which is an institution attached to Zagreb's medical faculty. He is a neurophysiologist, and that is what he used to teach at Amsterdam University before the war broke out. During the war he worked as a dean of Zagreb's medical faculty, and he was also in charge of the information office of the health ministry's medical headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have got what is called a disclosure note if front of me. And I have the following: During 1991 Professor Kostovic was the chief of the Ministry of Health medical headquarters information department at -- or in Zagreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you communicate with Professor Kostovic in 1991 when you were sending this material? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Having spoken to Professor Kostovic yesterday and today, can you tell us, as far as you are aware, what actually happened to the documents that were compiled from the e-mails and the faxes in Zagreb? What was the method and what was the methodology involved?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information office that was attached to the health ministry is now part of the medical faculty. They still have the original data. He told me that at the time records were printed by a -- using a method that he referred to as the VOX method. All the incoming faxes were photocopied and are still kept in the files of the information office in a section known as the crisis section, and this is within the medical faculty. He also told me that these originals are available for inspection, that they can be made available -- that copies can be made available for the benefit of the Tribunal. Likewise, he indicated that there was a need to track down the original medical files, because these are probably still in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did the professor indicate whether in actual fact there was a -- a separate database created for the patients admitted to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a separate database created for Vukovar and the Vukovar Hospital. Furthermore, the information office gathered information from all other hospitals across Croatia. They have records on all of Croatia's different regions and areas. They have also copies of case histories for other hospitals, but that is simply because most of the other hospitals were not under siege or indeed occupied at any point in time and thus still have complete records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are no other questions that I would wish to ask you in relation to that file, unless the Court wishes me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wasn't intending to go through each named person, because I've tried to cover that with the fact that they are either injured or ill persons within the schedule. So I don't know if the Court wishes me to deal with any additional matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, I think you came last week, and you very kindly brought this particular batch of documents, which I have in my hand. Is that right? Which I'm not going refer to, but it may well be the Defence may want to ask you some questions. But I think it is right to say just in general terms that it is a list of three groups of people, the names of which have come as a result of discussions with various sources such as the Croatian government Ministry of Health, the Croatian Mothers' Association, and Vukovar Hospital, the police, and the Vukovar-based NGO called the Croat Association of Former Prisoners of Serbian Concentration Camps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in very general terms, it deals with each person and gives a biography of them, their age, their name, and various other details. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I move on then to two other matters. You have been asked to return obviously to deal with what I will call the blue file, but in addition there were two other documents which have been served on the Defence at Christmas after you had concluded your evidence and you have had an opportunity of reading them. Is that right? One deals with the reconstruction of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital, and the second relates to court proceedings on the 26th of February, 1996, a criminal case against Kadijevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Veljko Kadijevic and others. He was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, but I think the document that says et al., but the document that you have, you've now got copies of that in B/C/S. I think that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. You're going to be asked some questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you planning to tender the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was going to wait and see the nature of the cross-examination, and then if it was appropriate to make application for it to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I suggest for ease of reference, because we have more than one document, that at least the blue be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And probably the other as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The large one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then we can quite easily identify which, if either, is being referred to by Dr. Bosanac in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. Perhaps the first one can be -- actually has blue file in the title in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you suggest a name, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I was going suggest the name that actually is at the top, which refers to the comparison between the Vukovar Hospital admittance register and list of victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: "(Blue File)"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be 345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the second document to be marked for identification perhaps could be titled, Biography/history of either killed or missing persons from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reference will be 346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, has a copy of 346 reached the registry officer yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour will be pleased to hear it's on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What a delight. Very well. Mr. Vasic, as soon as you have assembled the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel Miroslav Vasic, as you know; we've met already in this courtroom. I will be asking you questions regarding this chapter relevant to the documentation and reports you sent to Zagreb. And as for the contents of those reports, we'll see about that when we get the documentation from Zagreb. Mrs. Bosanac, responding to a question from my learned friend, you said that you entered the names of patients, their injuries, the date when they were brought in to the hospital, et cetera, into this electronic programme inside your computer. Can you tell me, what kind of data did you daily enter into your database in addition to names and types of injury?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Name and surname, father's name, date of birth, diagnosis, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I suppose you did that in the evening, so as to be able to --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made lists and then based on those lists, administrators entered those details. In the beginning of the war and perhaps even throughout the war it was a gentleman named Emil Aleksandar who did that. He was in charge of electronic mail and he worked at the post office in Vukovar. And there was also Verica Graf, who was our administrator and who also dealt with data entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bosanac. In responding to another question you said you received this data from the admissions desk, from the protocol of the surgical ward, and I would like to know the details. Did these details coincide? Did you compare them at all before you entered them for all the patients into the electronic system?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the details from the protocols of admissions, and in every admission these details would be taken down into infirmary records and they would be also entered into the case history of patients who were hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood that correctly, you found it sufficient to get the details from the admission desk to enter this information into your database?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The admission desk, as you call it, was actually our emergency department, our emergency infirmary. The procedure was such that everybody who came to the hospital had to go through this emergency infirmary, where his personal details would be noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These details, were they given just to this service of the hospital that developed this database, or they were accessible to third parties as well?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the computer service of the hospital that made lists for sending by fax and entered data into the database, these details were also taken down by the special service of the police administration in charge of the wounded, and they would forward this information to the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb. These details were also accessible to Red Cross officials, who made their own lists to be sent to the headquarters of the Red Cross in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they copy these details from the admission protocol, or did they make a copy in longhand?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not Xerox them; they just copied them, name and surname, date of birth, and such but not the diagnosis. They were not interested in the medical side. They were only interested in who was wounded, who was killed, and the personal details of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us about this database, the electronic version. Were the details entered into a specific folder on the hard disc, or were they copied on to floppies at that time in 1991, I mean your hospital computer?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the hard disc, and they were e-mailed on. They were not copied on to floppies in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Could you tell us about the reports that were forwarded by e-mail. Were they sent in the form of a letter, or did you have some forms to be filled in?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had questionnaires to fill in, and what was sent in the form of a letter were reports about the general situation at the hospital, our requirements for medical equipment, medication, bandages, and things like that, everything that's necessary to the work of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This electronic mail, did it operate in the way it functions today?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not tell you that precisely. That was back in 1991. There is probably some difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever send these reports personally by e-mail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would dictate them to the administrator, who did the typing at the computer, so I saw how it works, but I didn't do it myself. I was not computer literate at the time, to be able to do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is that since you saw how it worked, was there an e-mail address they typed in to which they sent this information? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, but I think it was a direct line that was reserved only for that exchange between our information section of the Ministry of Health in Zagreb and the Vukovar Hospital. I also saw the computer at the Defence headquarters, where I would also go sometimes to tell them about the supplies we needed. In October and November there was a direct line to that computer at the defence headquarters and the defence headquarters in Vinkovci, although I'm not sure about that. I don't think it worked exactly the way it works today, when you have internet and you can go anywhere. I think those were direct, secure lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did it work with the help of PTT traffic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- in fact I know that it was a dial-up connection, a telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you sign those reports, did somebody sign in your name, or did they go unsigned?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those reports that were e-mailed, I didn't sign them because I couldn't, of course. As for the lists of wounded that we sent by fax, some I signed, some I didn't. I believe I signed most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you check those reports that were e-mailed before they were sent, or did you just dictate them and they were sent on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean did I check whether they reached their destination or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, I also mean did you check the contents as well?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't check. I suppose that they reached their destination. In those times I really had no time to spend more time than necessary on administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me this: With all the reports that were sent from the hospital to this information section of the Ministry of Health, did you quote the exact diagnosis for every patient?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for those reports we sent from the hospital, yes, they included the diagnosis, as was the case with all medical institutions. But that information section also received reports from other sources, and if they received information about the wounded or killed from the police or from the Red Cross, then it was possible that those reports did not include the diagnosis. I also saw cases where only one diagnosis and one case of wounding was recorded, although I knew specifically that they had more than one injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How about the processing and collection of that information at the Ministry of Health of Croatia, was it more for statistical purposes rather than to determine the actual state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of statistics is to establish the actual state of affairs. At that time it was really necessary to find out what the situation was really like in order to establish medical needs and requirements. Medical assistance at that time in Croatia was organised at several levels, starting from first defence lines and front lines, field hospitals in the rear through infirmaries that were always ready to receive patients who had been evacuated. And it served the purpose of analysing the military situation and the number of the wounded from the view-point of medical needs. And we are now working on a project that is called an "Analysis of Effectiveness of Wartime Health Care" that is to be published in several medical publications. We, at the Vukovar Hospital, are analysing the wartime effectiveness of our work by analysing the number of cases during the war and comparing those cases to present-day cases of persons who are coming in for check-ups after wounding, and we have been doing this for five years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bosanac. I understand that you sent daily e-mail reports to the Ministry of Health. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 80 per cent of cases they would be sent every day, or if for some reason we couldn't send the report the same day, we would send it a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing that in mind, the information section of the Ministry of Health had no need to take information about the patients from the Vukovar Hospital from other sources when they received updated information from the hospital itself. They were able to verify if the same patients were in question by cross-referencing them with other sources, but you would agree that you were the most reliable source?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say now, after 15 years, how, using what methodology and procedures, they arrived at their own database in order to make it as complete and as reliable as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you then explain why, in cases where no diagnosis was entered in relation to a certain patient - I'm talking about the blue file - why wasn't your information used, your accurate information in relation to all the patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say now whether any such information was available at the time or not. In theory, a person may have been wounded in Borovo Naselje, for example, and never reached the Vukovar Hospital to begin with, so we had no records of this person's wounding, but the MUP or the Red Cross perhaps did. It is for this reason that I find it very difficult to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about those patients for whom we have no diagnosis in the blue file? Were those patients who were not brought into the hospital? Were those patients who had been wounded and were seen to elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to generalise. I can't say about each and every one of them. I would have to study each and every one of these cases individually in order to be able to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But there were a number of such cases, such as the one about Borovo Naselje that you described; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was possible. This database - I'm not sure whether you've noticed - is not about the Vukovar Hospital only, but rather it relates to the entire area, Eastern Slavonia. If you go back to the files you can see that there is information on Erdut, which is a different town, with all the data recorded. And now the question is: Was a patient brought to Osijek or to Vukovar, because the distance was equal in both cases. We should have files printed out in relation to each and every one of these patients, such as the files that I have in this document here. If you look at any of these documents, you can see information such as father's name, date of birth, profession, date of wounding, place of wounding, hospital admission, Vukovar or another hospital, the date when personal details were taken, is this person still receiving treatment, and more information like that. You could print a special file with all the relevant details on any given person. It is only once you've done this that you can go on and analyse this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can such printouts be made based on the medical files in possession of Croatia's health ministry; is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last time I was here I realised that there were some doubts about this, and this is precisely why I prepared this comprehensive document about all these wounded whose bodies were later identified at Ovcara. And there are medical files in relation to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about this extended database, was it not available to Croatia's health ministry back in 1991, because all you were sending at the time was information on wounded persons, plus their diagnosis and there were some who weren't even sending that, just their name and place of wounding.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the place of wounding and the person's name. In actual fact, it was based on our information, not just us, but, rather, also the Osijek hospital and the Vinkovci hospital that provided information for this database that is now in the blue file. We can now obtain case histories in relation to each and every one of these individuals recorded here. If, for example, you happen to be in Vukovar on that day and you were wounded, you would likewise be able to obtain your own case history and diagnosis if you so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if this might be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well then, Mr. Vasic, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate that Judge Thelin is unable to continue sitting this afternoon. We anticipate he will be able to sit again in the morning, and we think, pursuant to the rule, we should continue the sitting this afternoon. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There is something wrong with the microphones. I am trying to reduce the feedback, but -- I hope it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, may I now pick up where we left off before the break? There is something I would like to ask you about the diagnosis that you mentioned. You said that whenever a patient was admitted to the hospital in emergency, the working diagnosis was established, but you also said that eight different protocols were kept in relation to each patient. What I want to know is whether entries into these protocols were ever reconciled, whether they were checked for consistency from the admission stage and then all the other protocols that followed, the ones that you have enumerated for us.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean by "reconciled." Each patient had his own case history. They would be admitted, and their admission would be recorded. If they were outpatients, they would get a case history; if they were inpatients, there would be a temperature chart and findings attached to their case history. If a patient had to undergo surgery, there was an anaesthesia protocol also. I'm not sure what you mean by "reconciled".

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for explaining this. There were different medical workers who kept different kinds of information on a patient at various stages throughout a patient's treatment. The records that were taken at admission reflected one thing, but any records made during a patient's treatment were different; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases this was the same, but you always have a working diagnosis, which is the first initial diagnosis that is established when a patient is admitted. For example, if you have an explosive wound to the right knee, this can be a working diagnosis, but this can also end up as a leg amputation. There are various situations that can occur during treatment, and medical records can be kept in a variety of ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The reports that you sent to the information department of Croatia's health ministry were based on whatever initial information you received from your emergency admission; that is where information was first gathered. Right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It was for this reason that these reports only included information, the personal details of patients and their wounding, but nothing to reflect how their condition evolved during treatment. Right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, neither in the reports nor in the blue file do we find any sort of information on the release of any patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing in the blue file. If you look at all the subfiles, as it were, there are detailed printouts of all this information in relation to each of the wounded at a given time. If a patient was sent to a different institution, or if they had to remain in order to receive treatment, there were ways to add this new information to the already existing information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but the information is not complete in this blue file. We can only see when a person was admitted to the hospital, but we can't see anything about the treatment or the date when a person was released. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would like to consider now is one particular column from the blue file. I will not be dwelling for too long on this, but let me just remind you that you testified today about column 6, column number 6. If you could please turn to page 2 of the blue file or any page, because I'm not after information in relation to anybody in particular. Column number 6 on the right-hand side, which says "place, ZAP 1." You testified that this denoted the territorial affiliation of a person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on our information. This reflects where a patient was brought from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Further in relation to that, if you look at page 1, the first entry, it says "Omis," which is a town in Croatia. What does that mean, page 1, entry 1?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty. In order to provide an accurate answer, I would need the person's name and surname. I would need to check the information. But based on what I do know at present, this suggests that this patient was first recorded in Omis or its surroundings. He was probably a member of the National Guards Corps and he arrived in Vukovar as a volunteer. He was wounded on the 17th of October, and there is a description here of his injury. This information was entered on the 6th of December, and he appears to be from the Omis area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He arrived from Omis in Vukovar in order to fight. He was wounded, but this was only recorded in the Omis area at a later stage. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at the same column on page 2? The first entry is "HV," I suppose that means Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, in view of what you just said, that this column reflects the place of origin. Croatian army does not mean the place of origin; what can that mean?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that the patient was registered with the Croatian army, regardless of the place. I cannot explain this precisely; you have to ask those who created this database. You can understand from this that he was a member of the ZNG, that he was wounded on the 9th of October in Vukovar, that his diagnosis was taken, and the date of entry is the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand you can't help us with the contents of this document. It was made at the Ministry of Health, so I won't ask you any more questions about this. You are as competent a reader as we are.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me move on to another subject. You said at some point this line of communication with the Ministry of Health, more precisely its information section, could not proceed any longer through the dial-up connection, so you had to type up the reports and send them by fax. You said you sent these fax messages from the police station or from the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the format of that report you sent. Did it have -- did it have the letterhead of the Vukovar Medical Centre, and what approximately was the format of that document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was printed on an A4 sheet of paper, and it contained a list, number, name, surname, father's name, date of injury, and diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did it have a letterhead in the left upper corner, medical centre?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did it indicate the addressee?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was just a list of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you help us with this: Was there a date indicated in the left or right bottom corner?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that because I don't remember every report. There was a seal and a signature on every one of them, but I don't remember about the date. I suppose there was a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you signed these documents as the director?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I suppose it could have happened a few times that I didn't sign, but for the most part I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that you moved to typed-up reports as early as the 26th of October, that already by that time the other mode of notification for the Ministry of Health did not work?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely. We made those lists of the wounded even earlier because the police needed it for their reports, and the Red Cross needed them for their reports, so I can't tell you the exact date when we moved from electronic mail reports to typed reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But is it possible that it was in end October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Another thing, did you have an opportunity in Zagreb to look up those reports we are discussing now, or have they been archived and you were just shown the electronic version of the report that was made on the basis of that documentation, and you were not able to see the original documents?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there prior to this trial. They probably would have shown me the documents, had I asked to see them, but I didn't. I saw some of those documents on an earlier occasion when I went to Zagreb, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I did not express any doubt as to the existence of those documents. I'm just asking you if you were aware the contents. I hope we will be able to see what they contain. But my point was this: Were you able to compare the contents to this blue file?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't compare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I too am unable to deal with the contents even of this other documents that my learned friend introduced as an MFI because we received it only on Friday, but even that documentation is based on the records in the possession of the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Croatia. I just wanted to ask you in respect of this second file, did you have occasion to see the complete documentation underlying this file, this other one that was introduced as MFI --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the file which indicates the medical aspect for every single designated victim of Ovcara events? I brought those documents, and I analysed each and every one of them individually, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you could give us some information with regard to these documents if the Defence decided to ask you about each individual case?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you clarify one more thing for me, please. In this blue file, in several places we see that the date of entry is 1992, and even 1994 in some cases. Could you explain, perhaps, why some entries were only made in 1992, 1994, and even 1996?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite difficult for me it talk about it in general terms. I suppose that this was done after all the medical documentation was gathered, and based on the case histories of these people I suppose that they were only entered at that time. They were not entered, therefore, on the basis of our information sent in 1991, but only when those people turned up with their medical files. That is my explanation, but without looking at every individual case, I could not give you the exact reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Bosanac, very much. I have no further questions for you, and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions in this area, and we have to reserve our position for a later stage as regards the contents of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I will be very brief, and I will question you only about the record of questioning of a witness made in the Court in Zagreb. You have it in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said you were exchanged on the 13th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that a couple of days before that exchange you made a statement to the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show this document to the witness. Your Honours, the English version of this document is 2D01-0029, and the B/C/S is 2D01-0022.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me? Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you see at the top?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Record of questioning of the person brought in."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you leaf through this record. Go on, please, to the end. Have you looked at all the pages of the record?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to go back to the first page? On the first page is it written that you confirm for the criminal offence of armed insurgency, Article 124 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, that is the reason why you were questioned?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Record of questioning, 9th December, 1991, military investigating judge in Belgrade. For the criminal act of armed insurgency from the Article 124, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is the record of the questioning made from your interrogation on the 9th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that until I read it through. I can only say it is my signature indeed and that I was indeed questioned at the military investigation prison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was it really on the 9th of December?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. Two -- three or four days before the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at that other document.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It says there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I just interrupt, and I'm sure it is my fault? I have got document my learned friend is referring to, clearly a document from the Defence. But my understanding was that the cross-examination of the witness was to be restricted to the documents that had been revealed late in December and the documents that related to the witness -- or the patient from hospital. For my part, I cannot, as yet, understand how this document is being cross-examined on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain. Your Honour, that's very simple. Since we subsequently received the record of witness interview before the court in Zagreb, the fact of exchange cropped up, and we don't see from the record whether she had been interrogated before the military court. Now the witness confirmed this, and we know now that the record exists and the witness confirmed it is her signature. On the 28th of October, 2005, and you remember that, Your Honour, on page 810 when we asked the witness whether she was questioned or tried before the military court for serious crimes - and you can check that on page 810 - she said she could have answered only for the so-called verbal crime for something that she wrote about the JNA. Now we see that she was questioned about armed insurgency, and after her interview the military court issued instructions to conduct an investigation. That is all, I have just a few more questions, and I hope that by the time I'm finished you will understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Pause a minute, please, doctor. You will recall, Mr. Borovic, that the re-calling of the witness was for some specific subject matters; this was not one of them. It would have been appropriate for you to seek leave to raise this different matter. We will assume that you now do that and you are granted leave, and that's the end. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your experience in litigation of 35 years is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness: Could you please look at this other document, it's MFI D0043 -- sorry, sorry, my mistake. The number is B/C/S, 2D01-001 [as interpreted]; and the English version, 2D01-0019. Have you found it, "Request to conduct an investigation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, look at the last page, the reasoning. Do you see in the fifth line that this request to conduct an investigation relates to your questioning of the 9th of December, 1991? Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that. For the first time in my life though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek that these two documents be admitted into evidence. At the very beginning of my cross-examination, since I'm about to a wrap up now, I tendered four documents. The Chamber has only admitted one of those as an exhibit. Three were refused at the time, and the Defence was asked to provide a record of the accused's interview in relation to crimes and not in relation to a verbal offence. But she now appears to have confirmed this, and we have the statement dated the 9th of December. It was based on this statement that a request was made to conduct an investigation of this crime. We have a ruling, it's 2001-0010, this is something that we tendered a while ago, and this is precisely in relation to this request to conduct an examination. So all these five documents should be admitted as a single exhibit or individually because they are clearly linked. Let me say this again. We had those three documents that were exhibits. The first was information on military casualties, the second document was an official note, and the third document was a decision to conduct an investigation. Since all of this is in relation to the record of the interview of an accused -- and then there was a request to conduct an investigation, after which there was a decision to conduct an investigation. This suggests a link because the name is the same and the legal description is the same. It is for this reason that I would like all of these to be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution been served with copies of these new documents, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore, any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we do have an objection. We would like it marked for identification, please. I need to be able to clarify various matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. The additional documents tendered today will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regardless of this, can the Prosecutor please explain why I am tendering these additional documents, because we have just had the witness confirm that this is indeed her signature. It is necessary for these to be admitted into evidence so that I may be able to tender the October documents. This is a great opportunity, since we have the witness here now. You have been very kind in allowing the Defence to verify these aspects. Therefore, I think it would be a very good idea for the OTP to tell us exactly what their objection is about. I don't think this is a very complex matter. I do not need to have these two new documents admitted into evidence, because that would take us back to October 2005, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I'm doing, in respect of the Prosecution, what I would do in respect of you and have done on earlier occasions. And I'm going to wait until the end of re-examination to see then what it is, if anything, that is raised in respect of this document. So it's being marked at the moment for identification or they are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first document will be -- the reference number will be 347, while the second document will be marked for identification with the number 348.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no questions on any of the other documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosanac, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. I am Novak Lukic; I am counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I will be asking you certain questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, can counsel please be asked to speak closer to the microphone. We cannot hear him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about two of your statements, one was in the Kadijevic trial. I will also --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There appear to be some difficulties with my microphone. I'm not sure if the interpreters can hear me now. The microphones really are very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you a number of questions in relation to an interview that you gave to Canadian investigators in 1993, if you remember. You received these documents from the OTP back in December. It's an extensive interview that you provided to the investigators before this Tribunal was ever set up. Also, I have questions in relation to one or two other documents that have been disclosed to us. I also have questions in relation to today's testimony as well as the documents that we received from the OTP over the last couple of days. I will now refer to one of Mr. Vasic's questions because your answer did not strike me as completely clear. I am talking about the reports that you sent to the health ministry, the daily reports. What you would include in these daily reports was information such as a person's name, possibly a person's status, if that was available, and what you called working diagnosis established at the time. And if there was a permanent diagnosis, that was probably included in the same report. My question is: In these daily reports, did you inform the health ministry about persons by mentioning their names, persons who, between the 15th of August and the 20th of November, were released from your hospital? For example, such and such a person was recorded as being admitted to the hospital 10 days ago; we hereby inform you that this person has now been discharged.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please make a pause after my question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you had finished your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I had, and your answer has been recorded, too. I am about to ask you something in relation to a different topic. This is about the October evacuation organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres. I would like you to look at a document that the OTP disclosed to us, it's a Rule 68 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the court officer could please place 0D04-0108 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can have a hard copy, if you find that more convenient to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Mr. Usher, please, give one copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosanac, back in October, the 28th of October, and the transcript page is 832, I asked you, if you remembered - and I was talking about the October evacuation - if Bogdanovci was under JNA control at the time, and you said you weren't sure about that, but you did believe Bogdanovci to have been under JNA control at the time. That was what you stated at the time. Now, in relation to the present document, did you produce this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before? I believe you were shown this document at some point in the Milosevic case, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, I would need to go through it to know. This is certainly not my handwriting. I wasn't the person who produced this document. I'm not sure if somebody produced this on my behalf, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please take some time to familiarise yourself with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, again it may be me, but this is not one of the two documents that was subsequently revealed in December. And again, unless I'm wrong, it is not one of the areas that was agreed upon for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm just surprised Mr. Lukic is doing it now. It's just being mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have to say I don't think Mr. Moore is right this time. I'm talking about batch number 79 of the 22nd of December. This batch contains four documents that were disclosed at the time, and that's why I was surprised that Mr. Moore actually asked Dr. Bosanac about two of those documents. There were four documents included in that batch under Rule 68. One of these is her statement in the Kadijevic case; another document is her interview to the Canadian investigators, this runs into about 60 pages; and the third document is the one that we have on our screens now; the fourth document being the one that Mr. Moore referred to, the reconstruction of the hospital. All these were contained in batch 79 on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that resolve your problem, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't think it does. My understanding was that there was to be cross-examination on documents that had not been disclosed. I understand that there was a batch of documents that were disclosed in December. The Canadian investigation, I think, was cross-examined on at one stage, but I'm working from memory, it may have been another witness. Is Mr. Lukic saying that this is one of the documents that they have never seen before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is saying this document was discovered in batch 69 [sic] on the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have information it was disclosed in August; that's why I'm rather surprised. So therefore, it was not a document that was disclosed after Dr. Bosanac had given evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
