utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the very thing that I checked during the last break just because I was surprised when Mr. Moore told me that there were only two documents. If that's what it takes, I can provide copies, this is batch 79, dated the 22nd of December. It was the first time that we received this document; likewise, it was the first time that bee received the extensive interview that Dr. Bosanac gave to the Canadian interviewer. I just checked during our last break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I help? It's -- we've got it down as batch 31, which was disclosed on the 29th of August, and the receipt, I think, was in early September. So my learned friend -- if our documents are right -- may I just clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have got an acknowledgment by the Defence on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin that received this by the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really can't accept the fact that this is all a matter of confusion. I do know that we received a copy of the Canadian interview back in December. If the OTP can prove that I received the document in September, I would like to have that. But I think they should go back to batch 79, because that contains a list of documents and documents are listed individually. There, that is the whole point of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, again, we work from our records. It is document 999 on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which is that, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is under the heading, "A report on anticipated evacuation of the wounded from Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is the document that's presently on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as I am aware it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've been speaking of two documents. You mentioned one; I asked which it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the number that I have is concluding 0502. What the confusion for my learned friend may be is that we have disclosed it in August and we have also disclosed it in December, but it's certainly on the 65 ter list as document 999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And while you are dealing with it, what about the Canadian investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I just check on that? One moment, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Has my learned friend got the ERN number of that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, 0059-6194. It's the first page, and it has 60 pages, around 60 -- 70 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That document was disclosed on the 22nd of December and not before. So in relation to that document, the cross-examination on that we can have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, unless and until you can demonstrate to the contrary, it appears that this present document has been disclosed to you twice and you are looking at the second. But in any event, it is a document the doctor says was not prepared by her personally. So if would you like to move on to Canada, we'll have another effort there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I imagine there will have to be a break at some point during my cross-examination, so I will check about the first document, but I will move on to the other document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I will be asking you questions now about your testimony, based on your statements, your testimony in the Kadijevic case, and the statement that you gave to the Canadian investigators. Let us begin. Let me remind you that on the 27th of October you testified about the 18th of November, 1991. On page 682 you said that a large number of civilians arrived in those last days who were awaiting evacuation. You mentioned at the time, that provided a much more detailed description in your statement to the Canadian investigators, that you had advised those people not to go to the hospital. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why, what was the reason you said they should not come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the information I had then, the hospital should have been evacuated on the 18th of November, that means the wounded, the patients, and the staff; and only after that, after the evacuation on the 18th of November, the back-up hospital in Borovo would be evacuated. And only on the 20th of November, on Wednesday, the populace, the civilians would be evacuated. My position then was they should not come to the hospital prematurely to avoid crowding because the hospital by that time had no electricity, water, or food. We were unable to admit such a number of civilians. On the 18th we only had dry food, toast, and some tea for the children because a lot of children had been brought as well, and that was the reason why I decided so on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- first of all, do you remember that at that time, on the 18th of November, there was already in existence a collection centre at the Velepromet enterprise on the fair-grounds?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that on that occasion you did not tell any of those civilians that they should not go to the hospital, but that they should go to Velepromet instead?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told the civilians to go back to the basement of their building, and that the evacuation of civilians would be organised in the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you part of what you said to the Canadian investigators regarding this. But before that I'm going to ask you: Do you remember on the 7th of March, 1993, you talked on -- you talked about Vukovar events with Canadian investigators, Colonel Carter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that I remember now that those were Canadian investigators or Colonel Carter specifically. I have spoken since to many organisations and many individuals about that, but I don't remember a Colonel Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's actually Lieutenant-Colonel Jean Carter, a woman, who, at that time worked for an expert commission of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember giving statements to, for instance, the Commission for Missing Persons that was brought by Mr. Mazovjtski. I remember a female person wearing civilian clothes rather than a uniform, but I don't remember that she was either a lieutenant-colonel or that the name was Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask the usher to take this document to the witness? This document, Your Honour, was drafted simultaneously in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, please turn to page 45.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 45, you say? Just a minute. I just have to add about this document; I have already discussed it in the Milosevic trial. I have to say that this document was made after the interview and that the fax message was compiled subsequently, and I have not seen this document before in writing in its complete version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just give a clarification to the Trial Chamber? This is actually a transcript from an audiotape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw it in this form before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By virtue of a decision of the Trial Chamber the Prosecutor was able to familiarise the witness with this document before she came to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just go through a couple of questions concerning this document.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] is ERN number. [Interpretation] 45, 00596238. Here, Mrs. Bosanac, I'll read, and you check, as I read, because we have interpretation here. I'm reading from line 7, let's say, your statement. "At the hospital, apart from patients, the wounded, and the staff, many more people have come in. They had arrived back on the 18th from the Olajnica shelter in their basements, and they were all waiting for the hospital to be evacuated. I tried to dissuade them from coming to the hospital because we were overcrowded and we had no electricity or food. Marin Vidic, the mayor, and Zeljka Zgonjanin from the Red Cross in Vukovar were taking care of those civilians who had gone up to the first and second floors of the hospital." As far as I can see, this corresponds to what you just said, Mrs. Bosanac. Can we say that this reflects the reason which you cited back in 1993 for telling the civilians not to come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate you claim that you didn't know then on the 18th, that the civilians were also coming into Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not on the 18th. They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move to another subject now that you also covered in this interview. And it relates to what interests me, namely, the arrival of my client to the hospital on the 19th of November, the arrival of Mr. Sljivancanin at the hospital. In your earlier testimony before this Court, and that was page 680, you said that you returned to the hospital around 1600 hours after the meeting with Mr. Mrksic. You also said that you had seen - and I suppose it was that afternoon - you had seen Sergeant Sasa Jovic talking to some persons, and you told him to stop talking to them because you needed him for a statement to the Red Cross, the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was on Tuesday, the 19th, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That same afternoon you testified you had seen some paramilitaries, including the son of Dr. Ivankovic, trying to come into the hospital, and you tried to enter into a dialogue with this Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is: How much time elapsed from the moment, if you can recall that now, from the moment when you ran into Ivankovic until the moment when Zeljka Zgonjanin asked you to come out, which was the first time that you saw my client?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you now. I couldn't tell you now how much time elapsed. It's very difficult to say to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same afternoon, but which exact hour I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try another tack. On page 682 you said you saw my client for the first time between 17 and 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it refresh your memory if you tried to think whether it was already dark or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was still daylight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the same page you stated that you saw then men being separated from women and children and you saw with your own eyes, I suppose, those men being put on a truck?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I will also remind you, on page 683 you said you addressed Sljivancanin on that occasion when you saw him for the first time. You said on the 27th October before this Court that on that occasion he had told you not to interfere with things that are none of your business and to return to your office instead. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look for a moment how you described that when you testified in the Kadijevic case. Do you have your statement from that case?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I put those Canadians aside?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can do that. Page 5 of the statement you gave in the Kadijevic case. I want to ask you -- I suppose you definitely recall giving that statement before the Court in Zagreb, the district court in Zagreb, and that you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from paragraph 2. "Sometime between 15 and 1600 hours on that same day when I returned from Negoslavci to the medical centre, Major Veselin Sljivancanin arrived with JNA soldiers. From the first and the second floor, where civilians were quartered, about a thousand of them were taken, I don't know where, probably to the fair-grounds at Velepromet."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see that you mentioned the separation of men from women here. You just mentioned that around 1.000 civilians were taken away somewhere.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention it in answering this question. This statement that I gave before the court in 1996 was also taken in the form of an interview, as a verbal statement, after which the judge who questioned me dictated to her -- to his clerk what she should type up. I cannot tell you now why I didn't mention that, but perhaps if I was asked a specific -- if I had been asked a specific question I would have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But what you meant to say was that only men were taken away, men [as interpreted] and children were left behind?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked at that time why men were being separated from the others, and he told me it's none of my business. And I had the feeling, or I was even informed, that the men were being separated for a purpose. I think Zeljka or somebody told me that men would be listed or something and then women and children would follow. I cannot tell you how long this lasted, but the fact is that when it was happening on Tuesday, the 19th, it was still daylight, but I can't tell you the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it coming back to you now, according to your later testimony, Nicholas Borsinger also arrived together with Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you came back to the hospital did you see that this was going on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the time Borsinger arrived with Sljivancanin it was already dark, and I saw that they brought supplies, medical supplies, but I can't tell you anything more specific. I didn't go to look again. I think that by that time all the civilians had been shipped away. Soon after that was done, Borsinger and Sljivancanin took the lists, the soldier who had taken me to Negoslavci before came again. But whether all the civilians, those who came subsequently to the hospital, whether by that time all of them were taken away, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those from the first and the second floor, can I understand that you saw only that moment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only when the transport began, but I didn't see it all, or I can't tell you until when it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at what you said to Canadian investigators with regard to this same incident. Can you please take that statement, page 47. [In English] 00596240. [Interpretation] This is how you described that incident on that occasion in 1993. Have you found page 47?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from line 5. "And then I saw Sljivancanin. And asked him, 'What are you doing? Where are they going?' He said that they were going to Velepromet. He kept saying to those people, Everybody will go wherever they please. The Yugoslav federal army freed you. Those men are just going to be listed, and you will reunite at Velepromet. And you will go anywhere you want to." Now, I'm asking you: Do you remember that in 1993, when your memory of this was more recent, whether you actually heard Sljivancanin say it in this way?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said on that occasion when I talked to those investigators, and I wrote the same thing in my statement that I wrote in the prison. It is a fact that he came out with those words. He said: The Yugoslav army freed you, you will go wherever you would like, and he said that again the next morning at the meeting we had. And even at that time he was doing one thing and saying another.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you if he said it using those very words on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said exactly what I reported. I can't remember any other details as to who said what and when, but I assume that this is accurate, what I said back in 1993 in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just to go back to your statement in the Kadijevic case, a very short question about that. One thing I have noticed is that there is no reference to Mr. Borsinger's arrival on that day in your statement, is there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. I didn't go through it very carefully. I must have mentioned this at some point. I'm not sure if it was recorded, to be quite truthful. It's very difficult for me to go through it quickly and be thorough at the same time. He arrived in the evening, another doctor from the ICRC arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that eventually, but let's not dwell on this now. That isn't really that important. Perhaps you can have a look during the break and then just simply confirm afterwards that you make no reference in the statement to Borsinger's arrival on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be, because I did give another short statement about the hospital evacuation later on. I probably said something about that, they included that in the chapter that says "General Information," and then after that you had the document entitled "Reconstruction of the Hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're getting to that now.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't signed, but I assume, or suspect that it must be a part of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that although this document was not signed your words were recorded accurately?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could please have a look, this is how it reads: "On the 19th of November at around 1800 hours, Mr. Nicholas from the ICRC arrived and Major Sljivancanin arrived with him. However, 30 minutes later they left the hospital. At around 1930 they took me away to Negoslavci." Now, about this document, there is no reference here to Mr. Sljivancanin arriving separately from Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this document. But if you look at the hospital evacuation reconstruction, the short interview that I gave, you will see what the facts are. It's probably what I said before, and I suppose they just didn't realise that there was a need to repeat this information. I've given multiple statements before this Tribunal. I have testified a number of times, and this is what I remember about the exact succession of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hear you, Mrs. Bosanac, and I think I am making the position of my client crystal clear to you, and that's what I'm asking questions you about. You didn't agree with me back in October when I asked you about this, but now I am showing you documents indicating that he arrived, together with Nicholas Borsinger, on the afternoon of that day bringing medicines and he that was the only time he arrived on that day. Do you remember me saying that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the fact that you said so at the time, but you must allow for the possibility, since it has been a very long time, that perhaps not even your client remembers everything with perfect clarity. What I do remember for certain is that I met him on afternoon of the 19th, and it was already night-time by the time he reached my office with Borsinger on the evening of that Tuesday. What time was it exactly, I really can't say. This was the 20th [as interpreted] of November, even if it was 6.00 p.m., it was probably already dark. I do tend to believe that it was 6.00 or 6:30; however, upon my return from Negoslavci, I remember it was a sunny day - and my memory is particularly vivid - I ran into him along the approach road to emergency. I'm not sure if he has forgotten that, but one thing is certain: I remember that are perfect clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just draw your attention to something that you said on page 57 of the transcript, line 18, you mentioned the 20th and we're talking about 19; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about Tuesday, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you said a while ago, and as you testified on 856 on the 30th of October, when Mr. Sljivancanin arrived with Borsinger it was dark already, and you have just repeated that, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You also described your conversation with Mr. Borsinger, saying that he had brought some medical supplies and you were disappointed by the fact that he refused to stay there overnight with you. I would like to have a look at how you described this dialogue to the Canadian investigators on page 54. [In English] For the Prosecutor, 0059-6247. [Interpretation] Page 54. This is the bottom of the page. "This man named Nicholas was there too -- or rather, this representative of the International Red Cross, and this lady who was interpreting. Mr. Nicholas asked me if I believed that his presence during the evacuation was necessary. I was greatly surprised by this question. I said" -- and there is something that is slightly unclear here. "In Zagreb an agreement was signed indicating that he had to be involved in the evacuation because he was there on behalf of International Red Cross. He then said, 'Fine, he said that he would be there. I said it was his duty to be there because there were a lot of Croatian soldiers among the wounded and I was afraid for them. He then said he wished to warn me that if the JNA refused to allow these people to be evacuated, there was nothing he could do to prevent that. I became even more scared at this point and asked him to please make sure he was present for the evacuation." Now that I have read this out to you, this is your statement from 1993. Does this refresh your memory as to what exactly the substance was of the conversation that took place between you and Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He asked you at the time whether you believed that he had to be there, that he had to be present; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While testifying in chief you explained that you gave him a list of wounded persons who were awaiting evacuation, and you thought Sljivancanin took the other list that was there, that's what you believed; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the fact that he told you this: If the JNA decided to hold back a particular wounded person, there was nothing he could do to prevent that. What was your reaction when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I was at a loss. I couldn't understand what he meant, but I said that he certainly was duty-bound to be there, to be present. I can explain why I reasoned like this, and why I was afraid. Because in the case of the previous convoy, the one organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres to evacuate the wounded, there were a number of wounded Croatian soldiers who were afraid of this evacuation. They didn't know how they would leave town, who would be taking charge of them, and where they would be taking them to; and one of those wounded asked me whether I or anybody else could offer guarantees that they would be safe leaving Vukovar and whether I could guarantee that they would reach Zagreb safely. I said I could offer no such guarantees and that they needed further treatment and that they to continue their treatment as soon as possible. It was for this reason that I was afraid for those wounded because nobody could say at the time how exactly the evacuation would unfold or which route they would take; however, based on the agreement that had been signed in Zagreb between the JNA, the Croatian government, and the ECMM, it was quite clear that the hospital would be neutralised and the European monitors, I'm sorry, would carry out the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. You were racing ahead of the interpreter who wasn't able to keep up with you. I was trying to slow you down. I think he has managed to get there in the end, but if it's possible to go a little slower, it would help the poor interpreter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I just have one question, and then we can have a break. I believe the interpreters might need a break by this point. Do you remember on that day, the 19th, early in the evening, you talked to Borsinger, or at least that's what you say. Did you know at the time that on the previous day, 180 members of the Croatian army, or ZNG, had surrendered at Mitnica, people who were led by Filip Karaula, did you know that on this day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in prison in Mitrovica and I shared a cell with other women from Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this would be a convenient time for a break, Your Honours, or perhaps I can move on to another topic if you so prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I could give you four minutes, but I think probably your first idea was the better one. You're clearly wanting to collect your thoughts. I think, Doctor, we will have a break now and we will resume just after a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac, I will remind you of your testimony in October. I want to ask you questions about some documents that we received later on. On the 31st of October, on page 846 you testified that you had informed Mr. Hebrang that 400 people were awaiting evacuation and that there were a total of 180 wounded who required ambulances to be evacuated. You also testified, what I asked you about a while ago, you said that you gave a copy of wounded persons and those requiring evacuation to Mr. Borsinger and that Sljivancanin had all of the remaining copies. You testified about this on the 27th of October. Do you remember that portion of your testimony, or do you want us to go back to your transcript?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about evacuation lists comprising about 400 persons, and if, according to your testimony, there were 180 persons who required transport in an ambulance, not a bus, this would leave us with about 220 persons wounded or sick who were fit enough to be taken away on a bus; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, I'm taking this figure of 220 as a ballpark figure, and I'm putting it to you that not all of those were wounded. When you informed Hebrang about this figure, did you also take that to include persons who were not inpatients, but rather outpatients of the hospital who had been spending the previous days at home?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the number of ambulances that we would require in order to conduct the evacuation, I took into account all of the wounded and sick who were in the hospital or who came to the hospital on a daily basis to have their wounds dressed. There were many more wounded in shelters around town. But based on my recollection, their condition was not serious enough to warrant transport in an ambulance, since we expected that everybody else would be evacuated two days later from the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this figure of about 400 would include everybody who you believed to qualify as wounded and sick, those who were inside the hospital, regardless of whether they were inpatients or outpatients; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these people were in the hospital at the time receiving treatment. If you go back to my statement in the Mitrovica prison when my memory was still very vivid, I spoke about 396 patients, most of them in surgery but also in other wards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did go through your statement in Mitrovica. You mean the statement that you gave to the European monitors; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because that figure is referenced in that statement, too.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the one from Mitrovica; I should have it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The one you gave to Colonel Branko; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Branko. I mentioned the exact number of patients there. If you want me to, I can track that down for you. 396. 396, 200-something in surgery and about 80 of them in other wards of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to your statement to the Canadian investigators, page 51. For the benefit of the OTP the ERN is 0059-6244. This is what you said in relation to the figures, that's midway down the page: "There were those 180 seriously wounded and about another 80 slightly wound who were at the hospital. But there were a number of outpatients who had some documents with findings from a specialist, but those people were not on any of the lists. I thought that my father-in-law, my mother-in-law, and other such elderly people, as well as those unable to walk, would be in one of the hospital lists but they weren't." If I look at this, I see that on the 18th of November the figure mentioned in relation to persons who were patients of the Vukovar Hospital was 180 seriously wounded and about 80 slightly wounded persons. The rest being persons which you describe as persons you believe required evacuation as sick, infirm, and elderly; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not quite. You can read here that there were 180 seriously wounded person who is required transport in an ambulance, and there were about 80 slightly wounded persons who could be taken away on a bus. As for the rest, there were pregnant women or women who had just recently given birth and a number of other patients totalling about 400 persons who required evacuation from the hospital, plus about 300 medical staff, plus their families, on top of which a number of wounded persons also had people accompanying them and their families. Your client was very important for many of those. He was to decide whether they could join the sick and infirm. Some of those people survived the evacuation, but some ended up at Ovcara. Therefore, you can't hold me to every single figure. It's difficult to know precisely. We are only able to say now what the exact figures were, having obtained the figures in relation to the wounded and in relation to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, please just answer my question, if you can. You claim that the most accurate information is the one you provided in Mitrovica because your memory was still fresh; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should assume so, although in Mitrovica I provided this information based on my memory in the hospital. But not even in Mitrovica was I able to know how many newcomers there were or outpatients who on that day arrived at the hospital and applied to be evacuated, those who never were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us look at another different testimony of yours before the Court. You testified before the Court here that at that time - at least that's the way I understood it - you gave Borsinger one copy of the list of the wounded for evacuation and another copy to Sljivancanin. I understood it all happened in your office at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, look at your statement in Kadijevic case, page 5. It may be a small detail, but there is a slight discrepancy and I would like to understand. The third paragraph, halfway through the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just give me some time to find it. Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 5. Yes, paragraph 3. You describe how you went to Negoslavci in the evening -- in fact, you were taken there, you thought you were going to see Mrksic, and it was Sljivancanin instead. And then you say: "I was summoned to talk to Sljivancanin by him to tell him how many wounded exactly there were in the hospital, how many staff, and where the defenders of Vukovar were. He questioned me also where" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you've run ahead, and you're asked to repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not everything, from the "where the defenders of Vukovar were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From the passage about the defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I will repeat the whole sentence. "I was invited by Sljivancanin to talk to him about how many wounded there were exactly at the hospital, how many staff, and where the defenders of the town of Vukovar were located. And he also asked me where Jastreb was. At that time I had the list of the wounded with me from the hospital that I had prepared previously and that I had submitted to the International Red Cross." Now, my question is: Is it possible, as you said in the Kadijevic case, that it was in the evening in Negoslavci that you gave this to Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take anything with me to Negoslavci, nor did I have any special list to hand to Sljivancanin that evening. I had given him a list the evening before, before I was taken to Negoslavci. I gave one copy to Borsinger and Sljivancanin took all the other lists, but I wasn't carrying that with me to Negoslavci, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you say that it happened the way you testified in October?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I have a couple of questions about the meeting on the 20th; you gave a statement about that and you also testified about it. When you testified before this Tribunal, and that was on the 27th of October, page 692, as well as during cross-examination on the 31st of October on page 868, but in neither of these segments did you mention that you said anything about that meeting. I'm asking you now: Did you say anything at that meeting in the plaster room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember saying anything at that meeting in the plaster room. It was Sljivancanin who spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at how you described this on page 63 of your statement to Canadian investigators. 0059-6256 is the ERN number. This is a transcript from an audiotape made in 1993. I'm reading from halfway down the page. Have you found it? Page 63. "Major Sljivancanin came and said that I should convene all surgeons into one room so that we can hold a meeting, including doctors who were in charge of patients. I sent a nurse to fetch all doctors, and we gathered in one room that served as a plaster-cast room during the war -- that is, before the war. There were about 20 of us, and there were five or six men in uniform. It's the olive-grey uniform, the former uniform of the JNA. And Major Sljivancanin wore the camouflage uniform like the one our army had. And he said those men were doctors of the military medical academy in Belgrade who were going to take over the hospital, because from that point on the hospital was under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. "That Dr. Mladen Ivankovic, who was head of the surgical ward, said that he was transferring immediately to work at the hospital under the command of the JNA. I said that this hospital could not operate any longer, that all patients had to be evacuated from it because it was completely destroyed, and that, in fact, we should wait for the International Red Cross and the evacuation. Major Sljivancanin said that we should hand over our patients to the military doctors because they would be in charge of the evacuation, and that I was no longer needed there, so that I should return to my office. They escorted me back to my office, and that captain was still sitting there." Now, two questions follow from this. Does this refresh from your memory that you took the floor, after all, and said something at that meeting? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I said that on that occasion or some other occasion, I can't remember exactly. But that meeting happened in such a way that everybody just came into that room, the doctors and I and all the others, we were standing there while Sljivancanin was making a speech. He talked, I cannot tell you for how long, but he was saying that the JNA had freed Vukovar, that the situation would return to normal, that they would take over the hospital. And it's possible that at that point I said the hospital had to be evacuated because we had no electricity, nothing. I don't see what's important about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that anything is important or isn't; it's a matter of judgement. But that's your testimony, and I'm asking you now: Do you remember that he said on that occasion, which you testified to the Canadians, namely, that you should hand over the patients to the military doctors, because they would be in charge of the evacuation? That's what you said in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said that the hospital will be taken over by the experts from the military medical academy. I don't remember whether evacuation was mentioned at that point. I don't know. It's possible that I said that in 1993. This seems a transcript of the interview, I cannot tell any longer, but it's a fact that he said on that location that experts from the military medical academy would take over the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did perhaps later one of your colleagues, doctors, in Mitrovica - if you had occasion to see any of them later - did any of them tell you -- since you had been taken back to your office, did anyone tell you that the doctors who had gathered there had earlier that morning made rounds, Biba Kolesar or somebody?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time I had some information that they had made rounds and looked at patients. I can't recall anymore to told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you could tell me, if you remember, which of the doctors, Serb doctors was at the meeting then. You mentioned Ivankovic. Do you remember Stanojevic or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume it was them. I can't remember exactly anymore who I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Dr. Manojlovic maybe?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to yet another subject, that is, related to your testimony earlier today to these documents, and we'll go back again to statements to Canadian investigators. You confirmed again now that from what you remember - and that's what you said on the 25th October as well - that around 700 people were to be evacuated, including patients, accompanying people, staff, and others. Those lists, evacuation lists, we're talking about the paper, the hard copy, now that were given to Borsinger and Sljivancanin, you didn't give them to Hebrang, did you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you testified here in October last year, since you testified over several days, you said that you had a list indicating the place where everybody wanted to go. Was it indicated on that list the desired destination?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall anymore what this list looked like, but I remember we did ask people where they wanted to go. There were some people who said they didn't care. I can't visualise the list anymore. I don't know for sure anymore whether the desired destination was indicated by every name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But on the 18th, in those several days when you were keeping in touch by telephone with Hebrang and passing on this information, did you know then, based on what you knew about where everybody wanted to go, did you have in mind the figure of 50 people who wanted to go to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that figure, but I do know that some people said they wanted to go to Belgrade or to Novi Sad but I can't remember how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's forget about the number. In any case, there were some people among the patients and the staff, the wounded and the sick. You would not have included those people in the convoy to Croatia, towards Hebrang, would you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you precisely. I know that I kept constantly a record how many wounded I had in which ward, but I cannot tell you how many people did not wish to go to other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not go into speculation. There is another detail that interested me in your testimony, and it has to do with the document that you covered today, namely, the records of the wounded and the sick, the database. I will tell you now what you said about this database to Canadian investigators. It's page 21 when you mentioned it the first -- 0059-6214. This is what you said then. Have you found page 21?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "That computer was connected with the head office in Zagreb, and on a daily basis reports were sent. In the medical school at the university there is in existence this database that was updated until the 6th of November. However, due to devastation, this communication was broken, and after the 6th of November we have no data here in Zagreb as to who was wounded and who was killed." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have the data in that format, but we continued to send information by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, look at page 54, it's the same subject. [In English] 0059-6247. [Interpretation] "The computer was also in my office, but it hadn't been working for a long time. It stopped working on the 6th of November. All the wounded who were hospitalised received each a white nylon bag containing their temperature chart, their case history, et cetera." Now, what you testified today is that the computer either broke down or the communication line was broken, and that every day or every other day you used the fax machine to send your reports to Zagreb to the Ministry of Health. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did you continue to send these reports for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was probably sometime around the 12th or the 13th of November. That was the last time I went to Jastreb's headquarters, which was the only place that I could send reports from, but again I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you specify perhaps in relation to the 18th of November when the Zagreb agreement was signed. I suppose you were sending reports by telephone, reports about the evacuation. How much later did you stop sending fax messages to Zagreb concerning the situation of the wounded? Let me remind you, you said that on the 18th there were no new wounded in the hospital, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The last new wounded were admitted on the 15th, that was a Friday, I'm not sure about the following Saturday. On Monday, the 18th, a young girl underwent surgery, Sanja Vidic, who had been wounded on the previous Friday, but no new wounded arrived in the hospital. I can't really remember. It may be a week before this time that we were last able to send fax messages to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could they be, as you specified in October, on the 6th of November, all communication lines broke down and you stopped faxing messages to Zagreb. It's in all of your statements. You speak about the 6th of November as the date when all communication ceased?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We still had the fax machine, but I can't give you the exact date. Maybe the records in Zagreb will show which fax messages are still available for inspection. All I can tell you is that I have all of my written appeals. The last one that I faxed, the last couple of ones were phoned in, but I can perhaps go back to these documents to see the last date. This is the 9th, this is the 11th of November. This one wasn't signed, so this may well be the last one that I sent out. My last appeal on the 9th of November, this was signed, there is an official letterhead, and this certainly wasn't phoned in, this was faxed. So the 9th of November might be the date you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to take you back to what we heard today. I think there is a significant discrepancy between that and what I heard from you on the 31st of October; it has to do with the sending of reports and with what there was at the other end in Zagreb. You testified today, and we still remember this -- rather, I will read to you now what you stated before this Chamber on the 31st of October on page 863. It was actually me cross-examining you on that occasion. [English] "Q. When exactly did you begin to send those reports? "A. The 15th of August. "Q. On a daily basis? "A. Yes. "Q. You also testified on Friday that when you reached Zagreb and were eventually free, you had an occasion to look at some of those reports that you had previously written. Did you in fact and where was that?" "A. Yes. "Q. Dating to which period? "A. August, September, October, all the way until the 6th of November. "Q. Did you continue to send reports after the 6th of November?" "A. Yes. We typed them into the computer and we sent printed copies too, but I never actually saw those arrive. "Q. Did you ask Mr. Hebrang or whoever was in charge of those documents why the other reports from after the 6th of November were missing? "A. They said that there had been a communication breakdown, the lines broke down after that date, and the reports were no longer able to reach them via computer, and the same applied to the printed copies. Those that were meant for the defence staff, for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and for the Red Cross. All those remain in the hospital. I was never aware of anyone taking those files away. I think they all stayed back at the hospital. "Q. How were printed copies forwarded, by fax? "A. Yes, by fax. "Q. There is not a single printed copy at the health ministry dated after the 6th of November, but the appeals are there? "A. Yes. The appeals are there because those documents were preserved by some lady working with the European Commission Monitors," et cetera, et cetera. [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosanac, you were answering my questions several months ago when you stated clearly that after the 6th of November there were no reports, and this is what you were told at the health ministry, whereas today --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not even then. Well, you have just read it yourself, haven't you? We were not able to send our reports via computer, to e-mail them, but we used the fax machine instead, but I don't see any discrepancy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you ask Mr. Hebrang about the whereabouts of those reports, those after the 6th of November, and he said that the communication lines had broken down, the network was down?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are misinterpreting this. What do you mean by saying the reports are not there? I know exactly what it was that we sent. I don't know the exact date we stopped sending, but I know we both e-mailed and faxed messages, and we phoned some of the reports in. What I can't specify is the date the last report was sent, and I'm not sure why you're pressing this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only because my impression is that your answers to the Prosecutor in relation to the information you provided to Mr. Ivica Kostovic were different.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just a different perspective. There is a database they gave us back in 1997, which we are now using to get information on the people wounded back in 1991, because there is no other way through this Tribunal or the health ministry or the Red Cross that we could possibly obtain these medical files. I think it would be a fair and humanitarian gesture for these files to be sent back to Vukovar. There is no reason for these files to remain jealously guarded in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Verica Graf, at least as far as I understand your testimony, was the person who was entering this information into the database; right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, but she was not the only one entering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: She gave a statement to the Croatian authorities saying that the computer had been destroyed on the 14th, possibly 15th of October, 1991. Do you know anything about that? Is she wrong?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's wrong. That's not accurate. Maybe she meant that there had been a breakdown but the computer survived, as it were, and it was still in my office, later on. I later saw that interview of Dr. Ivankovic to the Politika magazine, where he discussed that particular computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you about the person. This arose from the set of documents that we received on the 22nd of December. Among other documents, we were given Dr. Sadika Bilus's statement. I won't ask you questions about her; I will be asking you something about her statement. But I will ask you this: Were you aware of the fact that Dr. Sadika Bilus of those days in Vukovar videotaped anything?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What exactly was she filming?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I remember seeing her filming some wounded being admitted to the hospital, but I don't know what exactly she was filming because I didn't watch the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. As Mr. Vasic has already pointed out, once we are in a position to further analyse these documents we shall decide whether we shall be calling somebody else to answer these questions or maybe we shall be recalling Dr. Bosanac. But this is all for the time being in relation to our Rule 68 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you have been asked about contact with Zagreb. The 6th of November has been a date that has been used in relation to the computer failing, and you appear to be saying that you sent faxes and contacted Zagreb in other ways. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to turn up the blue file? And just let's deal with the first -- the first page, perhaps even the second page. Now, we have got dates of wounding. It is the third column in. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If you move -- I'm going to refer to various parts. If you move 13 lines down, you can actually see it, it relates to Nustar. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 20th of the 11th, and indeed if we move on down to lines 25, 26, and 27, we've got the 15th of November and the 16th of November. There's a number of November dates.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How is it that these dates are incorporated in this schedule if the communications were down, or can you tell the Court how it was Zagreb knew this material and the date?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the date of entry column you will see. For example, Nustar is close to the Vinkovci hospital. This information was probably forwarded from Vinkovci, the information on this particular wounding on the 20th of November in Nustar. You see that the date of entry is the 24th of November, 1991. This was after Vukovar had fallen and everybody had already been taken away from the hospital. Exactly where this information was recorded and where it happened can only be established if you get a printout for this patient, such as the printouts contained in this extensive document. You see information such as where a patient was wounded and where his information was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was in the middle of answering a question, so I didn't mean to interrupt. But I believe on page 77, line 10, Mr. Moore was leading the witness on something, something that the witness had previously confirmed she didn't know. What is essential here is not how Zagreb learned about the document, but when they learned about it. It can hardly be extrapolated based on this that Zagreb knew about the wounding at this point in time. We should first be given documents about this before we can speak about it. What is essential is when these documents became available to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't see any difficulty, Mr. Lukic, I'm sorry, with the line of questioning here. It's searching for information - not putting an answer into mouth - and it is relevant to questioning that was being taken, an obvious question, if communication did break at an early date in November or even earlier, is how is there information recorded later. If that throws some different light on it, fine. If it doesn't, as we confirmed by the answer, well then we're left with the answer. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just ask you, please, to drop down the page. You see, I hope, there are three gaps for the diagnosis normally would be, actually I think it's five. But there are entries on the 15th of the 11th, 1991; 16th of the 11th, 1991; 16th of the 11th, 1991, Vukovar. Do you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I ask the question simply this: That if communications were destroyed, as being suggested to you, totally destroyed, how is it that we have these entries in the -- on the 15th and 16th of November relating to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the next column, the one next to "diagnosis," if you look at the date of entry. For example, somebody was wounded on the 15th or 16th of November, so the date of entry seems to be the 15th of March, 1992, which is at a later stage. These people were probably wounded at some time or other somewhere, but this wasn't information that we provided to Zagreb. It must have been a different source, the police, possibly the Red Cross. If you want me to, I can go through every single individual on this list. If we open the file, if we see where the person was hurt, I think we see where the information had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't want to take up a lot of Court time. You see, what has been suggested is that your computer stopped on the 6th of November, and therefore you didn't have an ability to contact Zagreb. And all I'm trying to do is, by looking briefly at this document, where we've got entries for date of injury, whether they could have been entered as a direct consequence of communication by telephone or fax. Now can I just direct your attention to five lines from the bottom, perhaps that's another one.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 11th of the 11th, 1991. If you look across, date of entry, 19th of the 11th. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if you look over the page, in the middle of the page you've got again other entries in November. All I'm simply asking is: Are you able to indicate whether, in actual fact, some of these entries may be as a consequence of you telephoning or faxes after the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's possible. Not only after the 6th. It wasn't always the case prior to the 6th that information was e-mailed; sometimes information was faxed, the daily lists. Those were sometimes faxed, they weren't necessarily always e-mailed, because the fax in the police building was used, the fax in the defence headquarters, as well as the one that was actually at the hospital while it still worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to move on to -- I have only three topics, I think. I want to ask you, please, about the Canadian transcript. You have been asked by my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, the fact that in the Kadijevic transcript there was a suggestion that you gave the list to Sljivancanin when you went to Negoslavci. Now, I'd like you, please, to look at the Canadian transcript, and I'll give the -- the page number, if I can locate it. Yes, here we are. 0059-6194, and what I'm looking for is the page which starts at 6251 in the English, bottom right-hand corner, number 58. Now, page -- if you look at the bottom of the page, right-hand side, page number 58. The top of the page should start: "Interpreter: But Mrs. Sarlota, who works here, would know it, I think..." Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to drop down approximately five questions, and the interpreter asks the question, because it relates to, I believe, Negoslavci: "I asked where Colonel Mrksic was." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll read in English and try and read slowly to assist the interpreters. "And Major Sljivancanin told me that he had been transferred to another task... I want to talk to you. And I waited to hear what he wanted to discuss... He asked me, 'Doctor, where are the members of the Croatian army.' I said I did not know. He said, 'How come that you don't know?' I said I did not know..." And then you go on to say that you "received instructions from the minister... that in the evacuation... the Croatian army should not be present at the evacuation... and that there would not be Yugoslav army either... only the truck will arrive with drivers... and the evacuation will be conducted by the International Red Cross... and EC monitors. He again pressed me saying: 'What do you mean you do not know where the Croatian army is. It's impossible that the army is not there.'" Can I perhaps abbreviate it in this way, and my learned friends can contradict me if I'm wrong, but through that discussion, as has suggested at Negoslavci with Sljivancanin, is it right to say that there was never any suggest by you that you had a list? I see Mr. Lukic agreeing. So I think the answer is "Da." Let's move on, if I can?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have we got an answer, Mr. Moore, from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I saw a nod and a smile, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps the transcript would be happier to have the nod and smile recorded in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's a quarter to 7.00, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is that right, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. At that time I didn't have any list, not when I was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Finally, I would like to deal, if I may, please, with the questions that Mr. Borovic was asking you about your interview, and the documents that were referred to. Let me just locate them, if I may. They were the two documents that were shown to you. They were compiled on the 9th of December, basically when you were a person in custody. Do you remember that at the military court in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I notice that Defence counsel was Captain First Class Vladimir Biskovic [phoen]. Now, had you ever met him before? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the allegations against you at that time, were you able to deny, contest, or choose anyone to represent you when it came to this allegation, apart from a person that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was a military officer who said that the matter was now before the military court, and that the investigation proceedings were underway. He told me that I was under investigation because I had been sending documents that spoke against the JNA and that I was free to put up a defence. I asked if I would be allowed to call Minister Hebrang to ask him for advice as to what kind of defence I could put up in Belgrade if I was under investigation, and the officer said yes I was allowed to, but if I decided to do that it would take a couple of days, whereas if I agreed to a court-appointed defence counsel, the matter could be solved quickly and I would be free to go to Zagreb. In response to that I said that of course in that case I agreed to a court-appointed attorney and maybe I could even defend myself. I just want to say that through those appeals and fax messages that I sent, and some of them I had on me when I was detained, I only heard in October last year that the investigation was mentioned, the investigation regarding the treatment of several Serb soldiers. While I was under investigation in Belgrade there was not a word about that, and even that court-appointed defence counsel told me, because I had asked him, among other things, to notify a relative of mine who used to be on the Supreme Court in Belgrade before the war. He told me that it was unnecessary because the only charge was verbal offence. Not a word was said to me about what Mr. Borovic raised here. That was how it was at the military court. And only last year, at this trial, I saw the official record made in December, or perhaps later in 1992, after I was exchanged, or rather released from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just conclude in this way: When you apparently signed this document, did you realise there was allegations about you inhumanely treating individuals in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further re-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I am in a position of indicating to you yet again that we are grateful that you have been able to come back, and for the assistance that you've given. There remains a question whether this will be entirely the end of your evidence or not, depending on what might emerge from the documents that come from Zagreb. And in due course, the prosecuting officers will be in touch with you if there is need for any further attendance. But in the hope that that may not be necessary, we would like to thank you, and you may, of course, now return to your own home and interests. Before we, I think, finish for the day, Mr. Moore, the two documents that you were considering, are you in a position to deal with those now, exhibits -- or marked for identification 345 and 346.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has said that she signed them and the basis upon which she signed them, and therefore we will allow them to be exhibits. We will not object to that course, clearly within the context of the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will now each be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a question whether the second should be under seal, Mr. Moore. It's a detailed list of patients and medical conditions, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The -- the document, the large document, yes. It should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think we had communicated that through to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid the Defence is at a loss now. We just discussed two documents, 345 and 346. I think they were tendered by Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my learned friend just said I did. As for the documents tendered by Mr. Moore, they are still MFI pending receipt from Zagreb of the documentation. Did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two documents which Mr. Borovic wanted to tender as an exhibit, the Prosecution wanted to consider them further, so they were marked for identification. The Prosecution has now considered them further and no longer objects to their being received. So the document marked for identification as 345 is now Exhibit 345. The document marked for identification as 346 is now Exhibit 346 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you are correct, and I am wrong, not unusual, Mr. Vasic. My numbers are mixed. It's documents number 347 and 348 under seal are now exhibits. So Mr. Moore is still swinging, but Mr. Borovic has succeeded for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 348 is not under seal. The document I was concerned about is that one which Mr. Moore still has pending, which really is 346. So if you will excuse me all for having got all that wrong, but I think it's now straightened. We will now adjourn. We resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
